title: Kate Berlant on Her HBO Special ‘Parmesan,’ the Joke That Made a Man Flip Her Off and Her Next Project With John Early

body:
There’s a throughline in Kate Berlant’s new HBO special “Parmesan,” and it’s not cheese.

	“My addiction? My phone,” the comedian says at the beginning of the hour. 

	With slapstick style and performative haughtiness, Berlant yearns for a time before cellphones in the special, out Oct. 16. Chronicling the hyper-niche behaviors that define our online existence, Berlant describes the seemingly inescapable embarrassment of wasting one’s life away in an endless scroll. She delivers verdicts on the great issues of our time, like whether to cover a baby’s face with an emoji or comment “PARMESAN” to receive a link to a pasta recipe. In one of the funniest bits, she talks about watching videos of “unspeakable violence” to “unwind,” like “gorillas fistfighting zookeepers, tourists being eaten by sharks.”
	

	“It makes me long for the past, when maybe you’d numb yourself at the local watering hole,” Berlant tells Variety. “That suddenly feels so quaint. You’d be with your community, and some people would be abusing alcohol in terrifying ways, but at least you’d be together, and you’d be forced to interact with other people.”


	She’s in an Airbnb in San Diego, ripping the “Home Sweet Home” pillows off the bed and couch because “they have hepatitis.”

	“There is this loneliness, which is palpable, and I do think it will drive people into community,” Berlant continues, “because we’ll realize that that’s what we need.”

	
		The first two words of your special are “world’s ending.”	

	Yeah.


	
		Would you describe yourself as a pessimist?	

	You know what’s funny? When I was going to shoot the special, I was like, “I’m not gonna talk about the world ending.” Do I really want to dwell in that fear that we’re all so drenched in? I am not a pessimist, I would say, but I think fear is the appropriate response to the times in which we live, so I would say I have fear.


	
		Fear of what?	

	Generally, I have hope and optimism, and I think there’s a lot of beauty in the world. But I think that we live in a kind of undeniably existentially terrifying moment, and so it felt like it would be insincere or bizarre to not address that ultimately, because I think it is the water that we’re swimming in right now. It’s a strange time, and that also has pulled me toward how lucky I feel to be doing live performance. To me, the beauty of standup is that it is an encounter with actual people, and we are seeing the death of the living arts across all areas of life right now. So I don’t think the special is dark, but I think it acknowledges some of the themes that dominate contemporary life.


	
		I don’t think people will be watching AI comedians.	

	I agree. It will never die. People are always going to want people. I was on a six-week social media cleanse, so I was off for the latest [round of AI paranoia]. I logged back on because my special was announced, and I wanted the dopamine hit. When I was on social media, I saw all the AI stuff, and it really pulled my feet under. And then I deleted it again last night, because I just can’t do it.




	

									EMILIO MADRID
	


	
		You said you just went on a social media cleanse. To what extent is your phone an obstacle to creativity? How do we defeat the endless scroll?	

	We are in the fight for our lives. As far as it being an obstacle to creativity — well it’s complicated. There’s part of me that’s like, “I want to understand the culture.” I love the youth. I don’t want to lose track of where they are, of what they’re looking at. I think that’s really essential. I haven’t figured out how to have an ambient relationship, where you kind of understand, but it’s not completely overtaking your consciousness.

	It’s an obstacle for all of us, whether or not you consider yourself a creative person. It prevents your relationship with yourself and with others. Certainly I procrastinate. My focus has been ravaged by this thing, so I have to reorient myself, and it takes a lot of discipline. I was in school for many years, and I always loved school, and I don’t think I could be in school now.

	
		You joke about having chronic back pain from being an “emerging talent.” Are there other descriptors that have been thrown at you that you’ve grown to resent?	

	Oh my God. I understand why people have said this, but I’ve certainly been branded a “weird comedian” or an “alt comedian,” “left of center.” Sometimes that confuses me, because I have always considered myself quite broad. I cross my goddamn eyes. I identify almost primarily as a physical comedian, and so my act, I hope, is broad. I hope I can reach all different kinds of people.


	
		How do you feel about “character actress”?	

	I think it should be an Oscar category! “Character actress” I embrace with everything I have. I was always going to be a character actress because I have curly hair and I cross my eyes. You’re either an ingénue or a character actress.


	
		You do a bit about incest material being too edgy for the audience. Have you ever told a joke that you felt actually did break a taboo?	

	No. I’ve never been drawn to being perceived as edgy, or in doing edgy material. I don’t think I’ve ever thought, “I went too far.”


	
		I find it interesting that when you ask comedians about their edgiest material, it’s often not what you’d predict. Sometimes it’s not racial or sexual material but, like, some random thing you didn’t realize was touchy.	

	This is really interesting to me: There is a piece of material in this hour that did anger someone, and I was shocked. There’s a joke I have about fathers being like a family friend. I was doing that joke, and I noticed two people get up and leave — center audience. I saw it, but I just thought, “Certainly it’s not about what I’m doing.” And then later I was told it was a man and his wife or partner. And he flipped me off when I said, “A father is a family friend.” And then in the lobby, he threw a glass of wine. I touched a nerve, and I was amazed by that.


	
		That’s wild. Do you know why?	

	Probably he’s feeling a lot of shame or guilt around his parenting.


	
		You talk about your sexuality a lot in the special, saying you’ve “succumbed to a homosexual lifestyle” in recent years. Is it harder to write material when it’s personal?	

	My comedy has always obliquely referenced myself; I’ve never spoken autobiographically about myself. The [off-Broadway] show I did before this, “Kate,” was a send-up of that. So this was my first time ever doing autobiographical material, or actually trying to work through questions about myself that I actually had. Was it harder? No, it just was the only thing I could do. I had done “Kate,” and that consumed my life for a couple of years. And then I was like, “I guess I’m going to try to write stand-up again.” I thought, “So much has changed in my life and in the world. I can’t just pick up where I left off and do that again. I can’t just free-associate and present these caricatures of a person without addressing what was actually going on for me.”

	So it wasn’t harder or easier. It was just the logical next step, because I had just spent two years doing something that was specifically not about myself. Well, it’s all about yourself, always, of course, but I just mean — I created a person who isn’t me. I have an Irish, abusive mother in that show, and that’s not true. So now I was like, “OK, I think I actually have to talk about myself.”


	
		Talk to me about the anti-closer. You hilariously refuse to deliver one final punchline, instead remaining on stage while the audience leaves the room.	

	I chronically struggle to get off stage with stand-up. There’s this pressure of doing a big closer, everyone goes ballistic, and you leave. There’s something inherently embarrassing about it, because you’re reducing yourself to this expectation of the form. It makes sense that you would want to go out on a huge laugh, or that you would tie things up and then leave. That’s logical. But something about it has always … I can’t do it.

	I was doing shows in New York, and one of my oldest friends, Doron Hagay, who directed the special, said, “You need a big closer.” I was thinking about that, and I was like, “It would be funny if I never left.”

	
		You say something like, “I’m gonna watch you for once,” and it reminded me of “Kate,” when you would linger in the lobby before the show with a sign that said “Ignore me.”	

	I know. It’s so funny because I forgot. You can just never get away from yourself. The same questions and ideas and motifs haunt you for the rest of your life. I hadn’t even considered that for my last show I was in the lobby as everyone came in, and now I’m on stage while everyone leaves.

	
		Clearly there’s something about the relationship between audience and performer that interests you.	

	Yeah, what is that? Performance is so strange. It’s such a strange encounter. You come on stage, everyone’s like “yay,” and then you leave. It’s so satisfying. I love it so much. It’s funny how everyone knows their role, which I think is really comforting about seeing something live. For me, the most interesting thing is disrupting that expectation. I’d be remiss if I didn’t admit that I went to a master’s program called Performance Studies, where questions about relationships between audience and performer are investigated.




	

									EMILIO MADRID
	


	
		What is your relationship to fame?	

	I can’t wait to experience being famous.
	

	
		Oh, stop!	

	As an emerging talent, I feel — listen, I am a ham, and always will be one, and so I love any opportunity to be a goof or put on a little show. If somebody comes up to me and likes my comedy, that only makes me excited. I’m not Mariah Carey. My life has not been interrupted by people enjoying my comedy. It’s been enriched by that. But having a persona, being aware of one’s persona — this has all been so chronically amplified by social media. I feel no issue being out in the world, flesh and blood. That’s fine. That’s not complicated for me at all, because I’m not Mariah Carey. Where it’s complicated is navigating that persona and being watched and performing online. That’s this new thing. It’s not so new, but it’s pretty new. That’s what can confuse me or shut me down: how to continue that performance on the internet.


	
		When you were workshopping the act and doing the anti-closer, was it ever difficult logistically? I would imagine that some people wouldn’t want to leave the room because they just want to watch you on stage.	

	People are remarkably respectful and understand it. People are smart. People know what to do. When you say that you’re a stand-up comedian, often one of the first questions you’ll get is, “Oh, do you get heckled?” And that essentially doesn’t exist. That’s a new, perverse obsession of stand-up clips, but that’s not real. It doesn’t really happen. Sure, it has happened in the history of comedy, and I’ve had it a couple of times. I actually had somebody kind of heckling my taping. There was a woman in the front row talking to me, and I had to be like, “Please stop talking to me!” That was hysterical, because it never happens except for that night.


	
		I think the heckling thing has almost been encouraged by the comedians who are putting out the clips. I went to the Comedy Cellar recently and was like, “This is not a participatory art form!”	

	And people are engaging.


	
		Yes. I suppose at many clubs, they have a warm-up act that does almost exclusively crowd work every night.	

	And crowd work is such an art form. I want to be clear: Todd Barry, Moshe Kasher, they’re comedians that do that so beautifully. That’s a different category. That really does exist. But what you’re talking about is a direct symptom of social media and of those clips, and people thinking that’s what going to see comedy is. But even if I perform at a club, most people aren’t doing that to me.

	
		You and John Early have a very beloved creative relationship. This year you starred in his film “Maddie’s Secret.” What are you two working on next?	

	Let’s just say we are ready to have a television show, and I’ll leave it at that. We’ve had a couple of — I don’t want to use the word “failed”: TV things that didn’t happen. Pilots that didn’t go, or we were actually in pre-production on a pilot when COVID hit, and then it went away. So we are back in the workshop, and we’re doing some writing right now.
	
		The desired medium for you guys is a television show.	

	Movies absolutely, and John is such a brilliant director and writer, and I’m so glad that he’s finally being seen as the filmmaker that he really is. But we’re currently investigating television as a medium that could work for us.

	
		Can you share any more?	

	I’m not trying to be overly mysterious. We’re really in the early — we do have an idea. So let’s tease the market: We have an amazing idea! We would love to make television for the people.

	“Parmesan” premieres on HBO and HBO Max on Oct. 16 at 10 p.m. PT. This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: Kate Berlant on Her HBO Special ‘Parmesan,’ the Joke That Made a Man Flip Her Off and Her Next Project With John Early

title: Diddy Moved to New Prison Days After Being Hospitalized for Alleged Head Injury
description: Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs has been transferred from his New Jersey prison to a new one in Pennsylvania, officials and his spokesperson confirmed on Friday
body:
Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs has been transferred from his New Jersey prison to a new one in Pennsylvania, officials and his spokesperson confirmed on Friday, days after he was hospitalized for an alleged head injury.

	Combs, 56, was serving out his 50-month sentence at FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey when he was rushed to the hospital on Saturday “non-life-threatening injury,” the Los Angeles Times reported. Other reports blamed the injury on an alleged prison fight, an account the Bureau of Prisons denied. Combs returned to the prison later that day — but that return stint was short-lived, as Combs was transferred on Friday to the minimum-security FCI Allenwood Low in Allenwood, Pennsylvania.
	

	“We can confirm that Sean Combs transferred to FCI Allenwood Low on Friday, October 16, 2026,” a Bureau of Prisons spokesperson confirmed on Friday. “For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not discuss the conditions of confinement for any individual in our custody, including reasons for transfer.”


	A spokesperson for Combs said in a statement that the mogul’s team appreciated the bureau “taking the safety and security of Sean and everyone involved seriously.”

	“His transfer from one low-security facility to another is an important distinction, and while we cannot speak to the BOP’s specific reasons for the move, it is consistent with a decision made with safety and security in mind,” the spokesperson added. “We are grateful for the attention being given to his well-being and hope he can continue serving his time without unnecessary disruption.”
	

	Combs’ time at Fort Dix was turbulent, particulalry after an NBC News report in late September claimed he has access to contraband cellphones to “scroll Instagram and scan nude and sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him.” On weekends, he has access to liquor that was smuggled in by guards.

	Combs was sanctioned by prison guards after the report came out for “disruptive conduct” and was stripped of 41 days of good-conduct time, delaying his release from January to March 2028.

	The musician is currently serving a four-year sentence after he was convicted on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution in October 2025. His legal troubles have continued during his incarceration. Just last week, he was ordered to pay NBCUniversal $477,700 in legal fees after losing a $100 million defamation suit over the documentary “Diddy: The Making of a Bad Boy.”

schema.headline: Diddy Moved to New Prison Days After Being Hospitalized for Alleged Head Injury

title: Katie Zacharia, Trump’s Press Secretary, Is Out After Five Days
description:
White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is out after just five days on the job.

	President Trump told reporters Friday that he would talk to Za
body:
White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is out after just five days on the job.

	President Trump told reporters Friday that he would talk to Zacharia about a new role.

	“I said, ‘When I get back we’re going to talk,'” Trump said, “because I don’t think that Katie should be made to suffer like she’s suffering at the hands of the press.”


	Zacharia, a commentator who had appeared on Fox News, had a brutal week after being appointed by the president on Oct. 9. She took over from Karoline Leavitt, who left to join Fox News as a contributor.
	

	Though Zacharia has styled herself as an “attorney,” she has since acknowledged that she did not pass the bar exam and is not licensed to practice law. She had a brief 14-minute press conference on Tuesday, taking only three questions, and on Thursday endured a grilling from Fox host Sean Hannity.

	“What I feel is I really stepped up to the plate to do the press conference, Sean, with very little prep time,” she said. “Given the fact I had been on the job less than maybe eight hours, and had a briefing book in the morning, I feel like I did my very best, Sean, to deliver for the American people that day.”

	Hannity followed up with a series of skeptical questions about her credentials. Zacharia defended calling herself a “lawyer” because she had a valid law degree.

	Her faltering performance led to speculation about whether she would outlast Anthony Scaramucci, the press secretary who survived just 11 days in Trump’s first term.

	In the end, she did not.

	“Records are made to be broken,” Scaramucci quipped on X. “But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”
	

	Fox News reported Friday that Zacharia would be “transitioning out” of the job.

schema.headline: Katie Zacharia, Trump’s Press Secretary, Is Out After Five Days

title: Eight VIFF Films That Deserve a Closer Look
description: The 45th Vancouver International Film Festival (VIFF) featured some high-profile titles, including Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” which has been ge
body:
The 45th Vancouver International Film Festival (VIFF) featured some high-profile titles, including Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” which has been generating awards buzz for star Julianne Moore, and Martin McDonagh’s closing-night black comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell. Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky” took home the Audience Award in the Special Presentations category.

	Yet beyond the marquee titles, VIFF’s lineup spanned 76 countries and offered plenty of discoveries from established auteurs and emerging filmmakers alike. From Matthew Rankin’s experimental take on Brian Mulroney to Tizza Covi’s portrait of an aging blues musician facing eviction, these eight narrative and documentary films approached familiar subjects from unexpected angles or offered a glimpse into lives rarely captured on film.
	

	“The Loneliest Man in Town” (Tizza Covi and Rainer Frimmel, Be For Films, Austria, Panorama)




	

									Courtesy of the Berlinale
	



	A melancholy and deeply nostalgic portrait of an aging Vienna-based blues musician who is the only holdout tenant of an about-to-be-demolished apartment building where he had spent his entire life. As he says goodbye to his home and possessions — which include vintage blues records, memorabilia and an out-of-tune piano — he ponders the prospects of a new beginning elsewhere, even as he’s firmly in the last chapter of his life.

	“Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney” (Matthew Rankin, NFB, Canada, Showcase)



	

									Courtesy of VIFF
	



	Probably one of the most psychedelic and unconventional historical documentaries in recent memory. Rankin forgoes talking heads entirely, instead remixing archival footage, animation, and music to trace Mulroney’s rise to power in what feels like an experimental vintage fever dream. Rather than examine the late Canadian prime minister’s political impact and legacy, the film explores how his image was built and how his party transformed along the way.
	

	“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” (Noah Segan, Sony Pictures Classics, U.S., Special Presentations)



	

									Courtesy of Sony Pictures Classics
	



	John Turturro plays an aging pickpocket whose old-school craft is becoming obsolete in a cashless world. After targeting the wrong mark, he finds himself entangled in a dangerous situation with a crime family and is forced to race against a clock to save his disabled wife. Segan uses the crime thriller genre to tell a deeper story about the nature of progress and how the world moves on, leaving certain people behind along with the shared values, ways of life and technologies they once trusted. With its melancholy jazz score, it’s an elegy to a New York that’s slipping away.

	“School for Defectors” (Jeremy Workman, South Korea, U.S., Showcase)



	

									Courtesy of VIFF
	



	This hopeful documentary follows teenagers attending Jangdaehyun School in Busan, which helps the children of North Korean defectors to navigate life in South Korea. As they struggle to adjust, many deal with insecurity, shame, trauma and discrimination. The school works to give them confidence, purpose, meaning and a sense of belonging, while also helping them understand what their parents fled. For a number of students, the full story of their family’s escape is revealed for the first time on camera.

	“Minotaur” (Andrey Zvyagintsev, Mubi, France, Germany, Latvia, Special Presentations)



	

									Courtesy of MK2 Films
	



	Zvyagintsev meticulously constructs a window into the life of Gleb, the CEO of a Russian transport company who occupies a sleek modern home with his wife and son, but there’s a clear disconnect between them. When Gleb discovers his wife’s infidelity, it sends him on a particularly dark path, with moments of morbid humor intertwined. In the background, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is on-going, and the military is scrambling for recruits. The town’s mayor pressures Gleb and other executives to hand over employees for the draft. His household becomes a microcosm of a broader societal moral decay, fuelled by detachment, indifference, corruption, complacency and the pursuit of comfort. A Cannes Festival Grand Prix winner. 

	“Once Upon a Time in Harlem” (William Greaves, David Greaves, Neon, U.S., Insights)



	

									Courtesy of William Greaves Productions
	



	Imagine being a fly on the wall at a dinner party attended by some of the most influential figures in Black cultural life. In 1972, filmmaker William Greaves gathered artists and intellectuals associated with the Harlem Renaissance for an intimate dinner party at Duke Ellington’s home, capturing their conversations on 16mm. Now completed by his son, David Greaves, this documentary offers an intimate time capsule of a generation’s wit, debates and unmistakable style — inviting audiences to spend an evening in the company of history.
	

	“The Flight” (Soran Mardookhi, NFB, Canada, Showcase)



	

									Courtesy of VIFF
	



	The downing of Ukraine International Airlines Flight PS752 in January 2020 killed all 176 people aboard, many of them Iranian Canadians. The incident devastated the families of the victims and shook the Iranian diaspora. Mardookhi follows three grieving Iranian-Canadian families who seeking answers and accountability from the Islamic Republic of Iran years after tragedy. Through stories the victims become more than just names in a news report or a statistic, but rather individuals whose absence continues to affect those left behind.

	“Diary of a Chambermaid” (Radu Jude, Ritual Films, France, Romania, Showcase)



	

									Courtesy of Film Movement
	



	Jude’s modern twist on Octave Mirbeau’s novel follows Gianina (Ana Dumitrașcu), a Romanian migrant working as a live-in housekeeper and nanny for a wealthy family in present-day Bordeaux. Her young daughter waits at home in Romania, growing more upset with each video call and each postponed promise of a return. At her employers’ recommendation, Gianina also joins an amateur stage production of “The Diary of a Chambermaid,” with scenes from its rehearsals interspersed throughout the film. The film is built on juxtapositions: the care she gives her employers’ son versus the FaceTime sessions she can offer her own daughter. An elegant French home against rural Romania. The performative progressive speeches by her employers in contrast to how Gianina is actually viewed. And her outwardly warm, accommodating demeanour while the thoughts she shares with her mother or mutters under her breath are rather different.

schema.headline: Eight VIFF Films That Deserve a Closer Look

title: Joel and Ethan Coen Reflect on Their Careers, Streaming and the Future of Movie Theaters at Lumière Festival: Watching Films on iPhones Is ‘Very Disheartening’
description: LYON, France — Joel and Ethan Coen have embraced the streaming boom, working with Netflix and Apple TV+, but they remain staunch defenders of movie
body:
LYON, France — Joel and Ethan Coen have embraced the streaming boom, working with Netflix and Apple TV+, but they remain staunch defenders of movie theaters.

	Speaking at the Lumière Film Festival in Lyon on Friday, the Oscar-winning brothers were asked about their experience working with Netflix on “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs” and Apple TV+ on Joel’s “The Tragedy of Macbeth.” Joel acknowledged that changes in film distribution had also benefited independent filmmakers like themselves. In particular, the rise of home video had helped launch their careers by allowing their early films to reach wider audiences and new markets. But he was less enthusiastic about the way people are increasingly watching movies today.
	

	“The joy of sitting in a movie theater with a crowd of people, there’s no substitute for that,” he said. “I don’t think there’s any filmmaker that enjoys the idea of working on ever diminishing platforms. ‘Oh, I saw your movie on my iPhone.’ That’s very disheartening.”


	Joel Coen also praised the Lumière Film Festival for bringing large audiences together to watch films on the big screen, something he said had become increasingly difficult in the U.S.

	The remarks were part of a wide-ranging masterclass hosted by festival director Thierry Frémaux, who also heads the Cannes Film Festival, ahead of the brothers receiving the festival’s lifetime achievement Lumière Award later that evening.

	Despite being among the most celebrated filmmakers of their generation, the brothers were in a self-deprecating mood, sharing laughs, anecdotes and tributes to the collaborators who have helped bring their films to life.
	

	“I always feel I am not worthy,” Ethan joked at the start of the masterclass.

	The filmmakers behind “Fargo,” “The Big Lebowski” and “No Country for Old Men” spoke warmly about their four-decade partnership and their remarkably straightforward creative process.

	“We’ve always written together,” Joel said. “Ethan once said the way we adapt a book is that I hold it open and he retypes it into a computer.”

	“That’s why we prefer to adapt hardcover books, because of the spine,” Ethan deadpanned, drawing laughter.

	Asked by Frémaux whether they ever argued, Joel described a process of bouncing ideas off each other. “Burn After Reading,” he recalled, emerged from a conversation about a movie they would never make — one opening with the typewritten words appearing: “CIA Headquarters, Langley, Virginia.”

	“And then we thought, well, why don’t we make that?” he quipped.

	The brothers were also keen to share credit with their longtime collaborators, repeatedly stressing that their films were the product of a collective effort.

	“Us being up here, we’re taking credit for what a lot of other people have done,” Ethan said, acknowledging cinematographer Bruno Delbonnel, who was in the audience. The French DoP worked with the brothers on “Inside Llewyn Davis” and “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs,” and with Joel on “The Tragedy of Macbeth.”

	“Something emerges out of the collaboration with somebody else,” Joel said, explaining that the same principle governed his partnership with Ethan. “The secret to that kind of collaboration is knowing when the other person is right and you’re not.”

	“I think we’re pretty pleasant to work with,” Ethan ventured. The reason, he joked, was that they had “very big egos” and weren’t threatened by other people’s ideas.

	Frémaux turned to producer Eric Fellner, who was also in attendance, to ask whether the brothers really were so easy to work with.

	“We’ve made nine films together, so I think the answer is yes,” Fellner replied. “But beyond easy, they are by far and away the most joyful people to make films with in the industry.”

	Frances McDormand, Joel’s wife of more than 40 years, was also in Lyon. Joel recalled meeting the actress while casting their 1984 debut “Blood Simple,” when she was fresh out of drama school.
	

	Thrilled with her audition, they asked her to return later that day to read with another actor. She declined, explaining that she had promised to watch her boyfriend appear on a television soap opera.

	“We were like, wow, okay, that’s cool,” Joel recalled, to laughter.

	The brothers also reflected on their long history with Cannes, where “Barton Fink” won the Palme d’Or in 1991. Frémaux recalled how “No Country for Old Men” left empty-handed 16 years later, despite subsequently winning four Oscars, including best picture.

	Asked how they felt about missing out on prizes at Cannes, Joel recounted a Billy Wilder joke about an elderly man who complained to his doctor that he was having trouble urinating. Told the patient was 75, the doctor replied: “Well, you’ve peed enough.”

	Ethan turned the punchline on their host: “Joel and I agree that your graciously having us here was your way of telling us ‘You’ve peed enough.’”

	Frémaux, backed by enthusiastic cheers from the audience, assured them that the festival was eagerly awaiting their next film.

	Asked which screenwriting rules they most enjoyed breaking, Ethan insisted they were barely aware of any.

	Joel had some advice: “If you’re a screenwriter, you should break as many rules as you can.”

	As Frémaux wrapped up the masterclass by reminding the brothers that Lyon would be celebrating them that evening, Ethan had the last word.

	“We are not worthy.”

schema.headline: Joel and Ethan Coen Reflect on Their Careers, Streaming and the Future of Movie Theaters at Lumière Festival: Watching Films on iPhones Is ‘Very Disheartening’

title: Who Is Emilio Sakraya? Meet ‘Fourth Wing’ Actor Playing Xaden Riorson
description:
“Fouth Wing” fans finally have their Xaden Riorson.

	Amazon Prime Video revealed Thursday that Emilio Sakraya will play the brooding male lead alo
body:
“Fouth Wing” fans finally have their Xaden Riorson.

	Amazon Prime Video revealed Thursday that Emilio Sakraya will play the brooding male lead alongside Esther McGregor as Violet Sorrengail, the protagonist and narrator of the fantasy book series. They’re the main characters in Rebecca Yarros’ “Fourth Wing” trilogy (which has two more books on the way), about magic-wielding dragon riders.


	In the books, Xaden is described as a large, dominating wing leader with dark, intimidating features who is highly revered by the rest of the Basgiath War College. He originally detests Violet because of past familial drama, but it doesn’t take long for their tense relationship to descend into steamy romance.
	

	Sakraya, a 30-year-old German actor, has numerous credits to his name, including “Rhinegold,” Netflix’s “Tribes of Europa” and “Warrior Nun.” His other recent projects include “Those About to Die,” and he’s set to appear in Season 3 of “One Piece.” In these roles, he’s gotten experience playing rebel leaders and performing his own combat sequences and stunts. Along with his action-packed TV and filmography, Sakraya is also a musician. As an electronic pop artist, he has over 300,000 monthly listeners on Spotify and has sold out tours across Europe.

	While BookTok fans may be unfamiliar with Sakraya, they are well acquainted with McGregor after her breakout role in “We Were Liars,” Amazon Prime’s 2025 hit adaptation of E. Lockhart’s novel of the same name. The 24-year-old actress also appeared opposite Nicole Kidman in Halina Reijn’s “Babygirl,” along with roles in Disney+’s “Obi-Wan Kenobi” (starring her father Ewan McGregor) and Freevee’s “High School.” In the novels, Violet is described as a small, frail cadet with dark black hair subtly streaked with silver who requires significantly more dragon-riding practice and precision than her peers.
	

	The official release date for the “Fourth Wing” adaptation is yet to be announced, but the casting of Violet and Xaden brings fans one step closer. There are several other prominent characters like Dain Aetos, Liam Mairi or Rhiannon Matthias who will surely be announced as production ramps up. Fans will have to wait and see if McGregor and Sakraya will live up to the tall task of capturing the brutal world of Basgiath War College.

schema.headline: Who Is Emilio Sakraya? Meet ‘Fourth Wing’ Actor Playing Xaden Riorson

title: The Avalanches Create Another Sample-delic Pop Masterpiece With ‘No Bad Memories’: Album Review
description: Without overstating the case, when the Avalanches’ debut album “Since I Lost You” arrived out of a clear blue sky (to anyone outside of their nativ
body:
Without overstating the case, when the Avalanches’ debut album “Since I Lost You” arrived out of a clear blue sky (to anyone outside of their native Australia, anyway) in 2000, its impact was like the arrival of the Beastie Boys’ “Paul’s Boutique” eleven years earlier: a mind-melting leap forward in the art of sampling, a sprawling and densely textured opus created from a reported 3,500 samples (and no live instrumentation) ranging from Madonna’s “Borderline” to old soul songs to deeply obscure tracks, along with snippets of commercials, film scores, movie or tv dialogue (particularly the “That boy needs therapy” line in “Frontier Psychiatrist”) and heaven knows what else. 
	

	It sounds chaotic and sometimes it was — at times feeling like both of your neighbors are having raging dance parties at the same time — but for all the PhD-level crate-digging, DJ acrobatics and plunderphonic science, what really set it apart was the songcraft and joyful, distinctive sense of melody.


	It was a tough act to follow, and some 15 years passed before the group re-emerged (as a duo) in 2016 with the equally sprawling but more song-based “Wildflower” and, just five years later, “We Will Always Love You,” both of which found the group using a wild array of guest vocalists, from Biz Markie to Karen O, Danny Brown to the Clash’s Mick Jones, and others. The sampling and sound bites are just as impressive but function more in service of the songs than as foreground.

	The group’s new album, “No Bad Memories” continues in that vein, with another raft of impressive guests — veterans like Jamie XX, Panda Bear, Karen O, Faith No More’s Mike Patton and even Carly Simon along with relative newcomers Portraits of Tracy, John Glacier, Barry Can’t Swim and others — and some of their best songwriting to date. With some 31 tracks sprawled across nearly an hour, it’s hard to pick individual highlights but they include the lead singles “Together” and “Every Single Weekend,” as well as the Loaded Honey-featuring “Final Credits” (which sounds amazingly like an early ‘70s soul record) and especially “One More Fantasy,” which pairs a Kraftwerkian loop with a soaring melody and high vocal from Carly Simon — it’s over much too soon.
	

	There’s a recurring theme throughout of what sound like ‘90s and ‘00s videogame and technology sounds and advertising snippets (the cover features an iPod and a floppy disc, with arms and legs natch, standing next to each other); if they could have figured out a way to make “Clippy,” the old paper clip-shaped Microsoft virtual assistant, make a guest appearance, they probably would have.

	But most of all, it’s one of the happiest-sounding albums you’ll hear all year — the Avalanches have a way with effervescent melodies and sounds, and combined with the energetic beats and humorous sound bites, the fittingly titled “No Bad Memories” will light up any room it’s in.

schema.headline: The Avalanches Create Another Sample-delic Pop Masterpiece With ‘No Bad Memories’: Album Review

title: ‘The Julia Set,’ Starring Chase Infiniti, Lands at Sony Pictures Classics Following TIFF Premiere
description: Sony Pictures Classics has acquired rights to Niki Byrne’s “The Julia Set,” starring Chase Infiniti, following the film’s world premiere at TIFF.
body:
Sony Pictures Classics has acquired rights to Niki Byrne’s “The Julia Set,” starring Chase Infiniti, following the film’s world premiere at TIFF.

	The film, written and directed by Byrne, was one of the festival’s breakouts, thanks in large part to Infiniti’s commanding performance. The “One Battle After Another” and “The Testaments” star earned rave reviews — including in Variety — for her turn as Julia Fischer, a math prodigy navigating being the youngest, most gifted student in her elite prep course, while falling into an abusive romantic relationship with her teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney). Amid those pressures, the film’s synopsis explains, “Julia must find the strength to follow the path she was destined to take.”
	

	Jason Isaacs and Gillian Anderson also star as Pascal’s parents, with Nina Hoss, Carmen Ejogo, Chloe Bailey, Nico Hiraga, Liz Lin and Alex Dillard rounding out the acclaimed cast. 


	“Growing up, I didn’t understand that people made movies. I thought they were the purview of the gods, that they fell out of the sky, and if we were lucky, we caught them,” Byrne said in a statement. “For 35 years, my entire lifetime, Michael Barker, Tom Bernard and their team at Sony Pictures Classics have made sure audiences catch the movies worth catching. I couldn’t be prouder to add ‘The Julia Set’ to their extraordinary library, and to know it will be seen the way movies are meant to be seen: in a darkened theater, together.”

	Sony Pictures Classics, led by Michael Barker and Tom Bernard, will distribute the film in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore). The studio is planning a theatrical release next year.
	

	“With subjects as wide-ranging as feminism, romantic infatuation, class differences, familial conflict, bullying and love, and even what it means to be a math prodigy, Niki Byrne’s emotionally engaging and impressive directorial debut gives meaning to living in the modern world,” the Sony Pictures Classics team added.

	“Seeing the enthusiastic response at TIFF confirms what promises to be a great theatrical success as well as cements that Chase Infiniti’s much-lauded performance in ‘One Battle After Another’ was no accident,” the studio’s statement continued. “She is at the center of this deeply rich, even suspensefully entertaining film supported by an amazing cast.”

	The deal was negotiated between Sony Pictures Classics and Gersh.

schema.headline: ‘The Julia Set,’ Starring Chase Infiniti, Lands at Sony Pictures Classics Following TIFF Premiere

title: How ‘Call of Duty’ Found Its ‘Modern Warfare 4’ Cast, From Mads Mikkelsen’s Villain to Prisca Kim’s Ri Ju-Young
description: Beyond bringing back Captain John Price and Ghost, Infinity Ward narrative director Jeff Negus only had a rough idea of what he was looking for whe
body:
Beyond bringing back Captain John Price and Ghost, Infinity Ward narrative director Jeff Negus only had a rough idea of what he was looking for when he set out to cast Xbox’s upcoming “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.”

	“I think our process is fairly unique in this way. I know some games do it this way, but we often start with a design of a character rather than anything too ultra specific,” Negus tells Variety. “We’ll have some concept art, maybe more, in terms of how they would be styled. But as far as the specific person goes, we do one to one likeness using our capture process, and often who the character is greatly influenced by the actor that we get in order to play the character. It’s very, very similar to movies. Sometimes they’ll have more or less exactly what they’re looking for and find exactly that person. And we do some of that, but it’s very much the opposite direction, too.”
	

	Beginning with “Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare” in 2007, the “Modern Warfare” storyline marked the first “CoD” games to break from the franchise’s original World War II setting. Infinity Ward’s “Modern Warfare” games have largely been set in the Middle East and follow the story Captain John Price (voiced by Barry Sloane) and Task Force 141 team’s mission to defeat terrorist Vladimir Makarov. That story will continue with the fall launch of “Modern Warfare 4,” which features a war that breaks out between North and South Korea.


	Handpicked by Negus and his team at the Activision-owned studio, the “Modern Warfare 4” cast is a sprawling lineup made up of “CoD” vets and several franchise newcomers: Sloane as Captain John Price, Mads Mikkelsen as The Archer (pictured above), Samuel Roukin as Simon “Ghost” Riley, Elliot Knight as Kyle “Gaz” Garrick, Young Mazino as Private Park / Park Jun, Luke Tennie as Lieutenant West, Warren Kole as Commander Philip Graves, Rya Kihlstedt as Kate Laswell, María Elisa Camargo as Valeria Garza, Kaiji Tang as Zhiqiang “Zimo” Wong, Daniel J. Kim as Moon, Joseph Lee as Cal, Julian Kostov as Vladimir Makarov, William Lipton as Corporal Joseph Dunn, and Prisca Kim as Ri Ju-Young.
	



	

					Clockwise from upper left: Barry Sloane as Captain John Price, Prisca Kim as Ri Ju-Young, Young Mazino as Private Park, María Elisa Camargo as Valeria Garza
	



	Negus, a veteran of PlayStation’s “Uncharted” and “The Last of Us” studio Naughty Dog with a background in live-action film and TV, has been with Infinity Ward for more than a decade. He has served as the narrative director on Xbox’s “Modern Warfare” franchise since 2022 and cast the second and third games.

	“A long time ago, when we had Samuel come in for Ghost and we were trying to find that right character, his voice has this much lower end growl to it,” Negus recalls of Roukin’s casting in the iconic role of the masked character Ghost. “That’s something that I think with a different person or a different way of playing it, it might not feel as grounded. But he somehow walks that line between the two things.”

	As Negas and the Infinity Ward team were shaping the main storyline for “Modern Warfare 4,” there where times where they would “rewrite parts of the character” when an actor was found that “had some extra qualities we didn’t know that we wanted.”

	“When Prisca came in, who plays Ri Ju Young, who is high up in the North Korean regime, there was a way that she was playing it that I think wasn’t necessarily what we were expecting,” Negus says. “I think we initially thought sort of grandiose bigger gestures and things like that, and she played it so small and so focused, it really became a lot more about a quiet power than it was something that needed to be much bigger and broader.”



	

					Luke Tennie as Lieutenant West (left); Joseph Lee as Kal
	



	The process also required a balance between finding the exact right fit for a part and avoiding typecasting, like when bringing in Mikkelsen, an actor known for playing a great villain, as the game’s main villain.

	“It’s a delicate balance with somebody like Mads Mikkelsen because he’s so recognizable in that way, as you say. But that was something we were looking for in this character,” Negus says. “Price wants to kill him and he’s willing to go to some great lengths to do so, and I think we needed something the audience could recognize, a wider audience could recognize, as quickly as we could. But at the same time, he’s such a killer actor. We also knew that he wouldn’t be bringing exactly what he did to other roles that we’d be able to shape it together and find maybe a new avenue to explore that common thing that people have seen before. So what it came down to is he was just the most right dude for the part.”
	

	While Xbox, Activision and Infinity Ward prepare for the launch of “Modern Warfare 4” on Oct. 23 (early access begins Oct. 16), Taylor Sheridan and director Peter Berg are prepping their “Call of Duty” movie for Paramount Pictures. The film is set to take place in the “Modern Warfare” universe, but Negas says he is not sure about whether that means there will be crossover between the “Modern Warfare 4” voice cast and the film’s actors.

	“That’s a great question,” Negus says. “Unfortunately, for answering the question, I’m pretty removed from all things ‘Call of Duty’ movie. But I think the simplest answer is whenever we’re casting, we’re trying to find the person that’s going to be able to best play the role and and have a symbiosis between who the person is and who the character is and so it’s a pretty simple calculus for us.”

	Pictured top: Mads Mikkelsen as The Archer in “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4“

schema.headline: How ‘Call of Duty’ Found Its ‘Modern Warfare 4’ Cast, From Mads Mikkelsen’s Villain to Prisca Kim’s Ri Ju-Young

title: ‘Michael’ to Receive Musical Tribute at 2026 Gotham Film Awards
description:
The 36th Annual Gotham Film Awards Ceremony will present the cast and creative team behind “Michael” with the Gotham Musical Tribute.

	Inaugurated
body:
The 36th Annual Gotham Film Awards Ceremony will present the cast and creative team behind “Michael” with the Gotham Musical Tribute.

	Inaugurated last year by Hugh Jackman and Kate Hudson of “Song Sung Blue,” director Antoine Fuqua, actors Colman Domingo, Jaafar Jackson and Nia Long and producer Graham King will receive the tribute for the film, which grossed more than $1 billion globally.


	“For our second Gotham Musical Tribute, we are delighted to honor these incredibly talented actors and filmmakers for bringing Michael Jackson’s life, legend and music to the screen,” said Jeffrey Sharp, the executive director of the Gotham Film and Media Institute. “Their extraordinary work captures the humanity behind one of the world’s most celebrated artists.”
	

	The tribute will be awarded on Nov. 30 at the Gotham Film Awards, which will be held at Cipriani Wall Street in New York City. “Michael” explores Michael Jackson’s journey from The Jackson Five to becoming one of the most influential musicians of all time, highlighting his life both on and off the stage.

	Also starring in the film are Laura Harrier, Juliano Krue Valdi and Miles Teller. The film was written by John Logan and produced by King, John Branca and John McClain. “Michael” is the highest-grossing biographical film of all time, with a sequel currently in development.

	This year’s Gotham Awards will also present Danny Boyle with the Gotham Director Tribute for “Ink,” “La Bola Negra” with the Gotham Vanguard Tribute and Laika Studios with the Gotham Anniversary Tribute. Nominees will be announced on Oct. 27.

schema.headline: ‘Michael’ to Receive Musical Tribute at 2026 Gotham Film Awards

title: Bones Found at Philadelphia Home Linked to 7 Missing Women
description:
Philadelphia Missing Women
                          Bones Found at Home Connected to 7 Disappear
body:
Philadelphia Missing Women
                          Bones Found at Home Connected to 7 Disappearances
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 16, 2026
                            10:52 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Startling discovery at a Philadelphia home that's been linked to 7 missing women ... bones were found on the property.
      
    
            6abc Philadelphia -- a local outlet in the City of Brotherly Love -- reports that sources say the medical examiner's office was called Thursday to collect bones from the Olney neighborhood residence on the north side of the city.
      
    
            It's still not clear if the bones are human or connected to any of the cases. Forensic examiners are still investigating.
      

            According to the report, 7 missing women have been connected to the home via videos and images recovered during the investigation. Authorities began excavating the property earlier this week.
      
    
            Luminol -- a substance used to detect traces of blood the human eye can't see -- was also used earlier this week.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            6abc says the house once belonged to Raymond Horsch ... a pornographer who self-published a fictional novel in 2014 titled "Empathy: The Memoir of an Empathetic Serial Killer." Horsch died last year at age 82.
      
    
            R.C.'s son -- Eugene Horsch -- was arrested in June on federal firearms and drug charges.

title: Six Flags Over Georgia: Goliath Had No Issues During Most Recent State Inspection
description:
Six Flags Over Georgia
                          Goliath Passed Most Recent State Inspection
body:
Six Flags Over Georgia
                          Goliath Passed Most Recent State Inspection
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 16, 2026
                            9:06 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Six Flags Over Georgia's Goliath ride showed no issues during its annual mandatory state inspection, according to the state compliance office ... but that inspection happened about seven months before someone died on the roller coaster.
      
    
            The Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire released a statement Thursday ... noting Goliath underwent mandatory testing back in March -- and "No violations, deficiencies, citations, or red tags were reported."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            From what we've gathered, Georgia state law requires all amusement park rides to be inspected annually -- and can be inspected more frequently -- by a licensed inspector at the owner's expense. ABC News reported Goliath passed its last three inspections with no issues.
      

            OCI also noted the ride remains out of commission ... and investigators are in the middle of a thorough examination to learn how Monday's fatal incident occurred. The ride will remain closed until the investigation is complete.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            As we reported ... Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died Monday after he was thrown from the coaster, hit the track multiple times, and landed beneath the ride.
      
    
            Hassan was at the park with his girlfriend and her family when he was killed. He was just 42 years old.
      
    
            We've reached out to Six Flags Over Georgia ... so far, no word back.

'American Pickers' Mike Wolfe
                          Leticia Cline Announces Split ...
                          'Silence Has Cost Me'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 16, 2026
                            11:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            "American Pickers" star Mike Wolfe and his girlfriend Leticia Cline have split, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Leticia announced on social media that the 7-year relationship was over. She said, “For the past two months I’ve been trying to come to terms with things that have left me absolutely devastated.”
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            “While the world continues to see one version of someone, I’ve been living with a very different reality,” she said. Leticia added she's kept so much private over the past 10 years ... “things I witnessed, things I experienced, and things I stayed silent about because I loved someone and believed I was protecting him.” 
      

            She said she now realizes that “silence has cost me.” 
      
    
            “What I will say is that the person the public knows and the person I knew behind closed doors are not the same,” she added.  Leticia said she was still processing how to move forward. 
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            As TMZ first reported, Mike and Leticia were first linked together in early 2021 … shortly after his ex-wife Jodi Wolfe filed for divorce in November 2020 after a decade of marriage. In court docs, she said they split months before her filing.

title: Oregon School Shooting: Community Rallies Around Slain 5-Year-Old's Family
description:
Oregon School Shooting
                          Donations Pour In for 5-Year-Old's Family
body:
Oregon School Shooting
                          Donations Pour In for 5-Year-Old's Family
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 16, 2026
                            9:35 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The community in Bend, Oregon, is rallying around the family of a 5-year-old boy killed in Thursday's horrific elementary school shooting ... raising tens of thousands of dollars to help his grieving loved ones.
      
    
            A Meal Train fundraiser has been set up for the family of Rhoam Summer, with donations pouring in as the community works toward a $100,000 goal ... already surpassing $60,000.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            And money isn't the only support being offered ... community members have also arranged to deliver meals to the Summer family every day from October 18 through December 22, helping ease the burden of everyday responsibilities during an unimaginable time.
      

            The fundraiser describes Rhoam as a sweet little boy whose family is now facing a loss no parent should ever have to endure ... with organizers hoping to give his loved ones time to grieve.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... Rhoam was one of three children killed when a 16-year-old gunman opened fire Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School. An 8-year-old, an 11-year-old and a teacher were also killed.
      
    
            The gunman was ultimately shot and killed by a civilian -- believed to be the father of a student -- who chased him into the school ... while another man who tried to stop the shooter narrowly escaped a barrage of bullets that tore through his truck.
      
    
            For now ... the community is making sure Rhoam's family doesn't have to face the days ahead alone.
